card: Diminutive suffixes make things small or dear: **дом → до́мик**, **рука́ → ру́чка**, **ма́ма → ма́мочка**, **вода́ → води́чка**. They carry warmth (or irony) more than size. Names have whole families: **Ива́н → Ва́ня → Ва́нечка**.

sections.body: Russians use diminutives all the time, especially with children, with food and in polite requests: **Мину́точку!**, **Ча́ю? Ча́йку?** Recognising the tone matters more than producing every form.

sections.title: Tone
sections.body: A diminutive can be tender (**со́лнышко** for a child), polite (**Подожди́те мину́точку**), childish, or ironic (**Ну и пого́дка!**). Adjectives have them too: **ма́ленький → малю́сенький**, **хоро́ший → хоро́шенький** (*pretty*).

sections.title: Words that aren't small any more
sections.body: Many diminutives have become ordinary words with their own meaning: **ру́чка** (*a pen*, not only a small hand), **но́жка** (*the leg of a table*), **ча́шка**, **бу́лочка** (*a bun*). Don't undo them.

examples.ru: Мы сня́ли ма́ленький до́мик у мо́ря.
examples.en: We rented a little house by the sea.
